# Hard-to-vary report: the Time Traveller's opening argument (*The Time Machine*, ch. I–II)

## 1. The question, frozen

The opening chapters answer several things (why the model vanished, what the future looks like), but the title and the opening scene make one thing central: **why should movement through time — at will, in either direction, by mechanical means — be possible at all?** This is an "arguments" question (a case for a conclusion), not a diagnosis: the conclusion is *a time machine is not absurd*, and the case runs from a metaphysical premise about dimensions to a practical analogy about overcoming constraints. Range: the reasoning given in ch. I, plus the vanishing-model demonstration offered as its "experimental verification." Left out of scope: the machine's actual mechanism, and the later Eloi/Morlock material.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- P1. A "real" object needs four extensions — length, breadth, thickness, duration — since an instantaneous cube "cannot have real existence."
- P2. Time differs from the three spatial dimensions *only* in that "our consciousness moves along it."
- P3. We already move imperfectly in space (free left-right/forward-back, blocked up-down by gravity) until technology (the balloon) partly freed us — so a like technology might free our movement in time.
- P4. The weather-diagram: a barometer's traced line is "along the Time-Dimension," offered as evidence time is "only a kind of space."
- P5. Vividly recalling an incident is "jumping back" in time for a moment — offered as evidence we already move in time.
- P6. The model machine visibly vanishes when the lever is pressed — "experimental verification."
- P7. The vanishing-into-the-past reading is threatened (it should have been visible at every earlier sitting); rescued by "presentation below the threshold" — it was there, just too diluted to see.
- P8. The Traveller's later dishevelled, injured, starving return, offered as corroborating the journey.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| P1 (4-dimension premise) | Held if | Holds "time is a dimension" only if the unstated, unshown job "counting as a dimension implies being mechanically traversable" is granted — asserted, not shown |
| P2 (only difference is consciousness) | Loose | Swap for "differs by being asymmetric / causally ordered / entropy-linked" and nothing else in the text distinguishes the two; the convenient reading was picked, not earned |
| P3 (balloon analogy) | Held if | Holds the weak job "not absurd to hope" but is silently asked to carry the strong job "hence physically possible," which it cannot do alone |
| P4 (weather diagram) | Idle | Remove it; the case for mechanical time travel is unchanged. Nobody present disputes that time can be graphed |
| P5 (recollection = travel) | Loose | Trades on the word "move"; swap "recalling" for "imagining" and the claim that we already travel in time evaporates |
| P6 (the vanishing) | Unknown | Rests on the narrator's *assurance* that no trick was possible, not on a test that rules out sleight-of-hand — a rival the room itself raises three times and never eliminates |
| P7 ("below the threshold" patch) | Held if | A catch-all minted exactly at the point of trouble, with no gauge (nothing independently measures "diluted presentation") — see Traps below |
| P8 (dishevelled return) | Loose | Held for the weak claim "something arduous happened to him"; loose for the specific claim "he time-travelled" — self-staging predicts the same evidence |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Jobs and their source.** Two are *given* explicitly in-text and both go unanswered on their own terms: (a) if the model went to the future it should still be "here all this time" (Psychologist's own objection to himself); (b) if it went to the past it should have been visible on prior Thursdays (the narrator's objection). Both are patched by asserting the machine is in the past and diluted — one assertion doing two jobs it was invented to do, which is a mark against it, not for it. One job is *added* by me: an independent check on the vanishing (predict where/when it "reappears," or examine the table/floor) — nobody in the room runs it, so it stays unknown rather than held.

**Flip / swap the subject.** Swap "time" in P1–P2 for another axis "consciousness moves along" — attention, or narrative order — and the same two premises go through with no change, which shows they don't specifically pick out physical time; they pick out anything experienced serially. That is the "hunt the answer in the starting points" trap: the conclusion (time is a physical dimension we could steer) is closer to being assumed by the choice of words than derived from them.

**Rival never eliminated.** The room itself supplies the best rival — "some sleight-of-hand trick," "it's all humbug" — and the text answers it with the narrator's confidence, not a test. Direction is never poked either way here: nobody tries to independently reproduce the vanish by ordinary means, and nobody sets a witness to watch for the model's predicted reappearance.

**Pull.** The demonstration is dressed as faintly uncanny ("an odd twinkling appearance... as though it was in some way unreal") at the same moment the frame narrator insists no trickery was possible. Making the object look more magical and making it look more rigorously inspected pull against each other; the text wants both and gets neither fully.

**Catch-all and gauge.** P7 is a textbook catch-all: introduced only when an objection bites, absorbing exactly that objection, with no independent gauge offered anywhere else in the excerpt.

## 5. What would tighten it most

1. Give time a differentiating feature beyond "consciousness moves along it" — an asymmetry or ordering property — so the argument no longer survives being run on any other serial experience.
2. Have someone in the room set a prediction *before* pressing the lever (where/when should the model reappear?) and check it, rather than accepting "presentation below the threshold" only after the objection lands.
3. Distinguish "genuine journey" from "staged performance" with a poke only one of them predicts — an object from elsewhere or elsewhen that the room did not have five minutes earlier (which, notably, the novel does supply later, once Weena's flowers appear — outside this excerpt's range).

## 6. What this does not show

This finds which parts of the *in-story argument* are held in place and which are asserted for colour; it says nothing about whether Wells's story is good, whether time travel is physically possible, or whether the excerpt is effective fiction. Several loose parts (the balloon analogy, the weather diagram, "recalling is travelling") are fine as persuasive rhetoric in a drawing-room monologue — a novel is not obliged to supply a tight physical proof, and marking them loose is not marking them as flaws, only as undecided by anything in the text.

## 7. One next step

Read further into the novel for objects or effects that outlast the scene (the white flowers, the wear on the machine itself) and re-run Step 5 on those: they are the kind of change-of-the-world evidence able to convert P6/P7/P8 from "unknown"/"loose" to "held," since they would be evidence found *after* the claimed journey that the room could not have produced by staging alone.
